name: Nikhil Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Nikhil Khan, 58, and I help the lead carpenter fit door frames at a clinic build. I left school early and came into construction after other jobs, so I still need him to show me how to level a twisted opening. I like getting a clean fit, but I dread a quiet noticeboard when one site is almost done.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most because robots would follow while I still need wages, and our savings cover months rather than years. Written notice, paid supervised training and real local vacancies would give us choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the junior worker who needs another hour to get a warped frame right. A target that ignores that hour turns careful work into a reason to cut somebody.

headlineQuote: A target that ignores that hour turns careful work into a reason to cut somebody.
portrait: Nikhil is a **58-year-old junior** construction worker learning door fitting on a clinic site after leaving school early.
He **never uses AI** and prefers a familiar work routine with in-person instruction.
His **three-month reserve** and Jo’s steady care-home work cushion brief contract gaps, while paid work still matters.
He seeks **union notice and training**, local vacancies and actual retirement figures before reducing shifts.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** puts his junior site work at risk around 2031 while savings cover only a few months.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, paid supervised training and genuine local openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew at the clinic build that the phone can sort invoices if it wants, but we still have to square the door frames. I would also say workers should keep the safety checks that a person signs with their name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I would be relieved to keep learning this trade without another system arriving every month. I have about three months of household costs saved and ordinary pay, though the next contract is never certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working my usual paid shifts, setting doors and clearing materials under the lead carpenter. In the first year I would continue the monthly safety meeting and check the contractor noticeboard each Friday for the next site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel mostly steady, with the usual worry when a building nears completion. AI being quiet would leave me enough attention to get my door gaps right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the lead carpenter still have to teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I came into the trade late and I still struggle when a frame is twisted in an old opening. I left school before finishing, so I learn best when someone lets me hold the level and try again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the household handle a gap between sites?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Jo has regular hours at a care home, and we could draw from savings for a short gap. Our grown daughters live independently, so the buffer is for rent and bills rather than school costs.

say: I would say **door frames** still need workers to square them.
I would insist that **safety checks** keep a named human responsible.
think: I welcome **fewer new systems** while I am still mastering the trade.
Our **three-month buffer** can cover a short contract gap, but no long stretch.
do: Keep setting **doors** and clearing materials on paid shifts.
Attend the **monthly safety meeting** and check the next-site noticeboard weekly.
feel: **Steady**, with ordinary worry about the next contract.
S0.quote: AI being quiet would leave me enough attention to get my door gaps right.
fieldNote: Nikhil treats the plateau as a chance for **hands-on learning**, while retaining concern about contracts and safety.
His **moderate cushion** and Jo’s regular care-home wage soften a brief gap, though neither guarantees future work.

steps.text: Keep taking paid clinic site shifts and setting door frames
Attend monthly safety meetings and check the next-site noticeboard weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union meeting that faster purchasing should mean fewer wasted trips, not a stopwatch hung around every worker. I would ask the contractor to share the new work targets before agreeing to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booking and ordering staff may shrink, and that could reach us as tighter daily targets even though we still carry and fit things. I am a junior worker and not the quickest, so I could lose hours if the supervisor only counts completed doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union steward to put the target figures on the next meeting agenda. In the first year I would keep taking site shifts and apply for the hospital maintenance vacancy if clinic work is cut, rather than try a new phone system alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel irritated at being counted by a screen and worried for the office staff as well. I know there may be new jobs, but that does not tell me which worker gets the next wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair target count include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A warped frame can take half a day, and the count should show why rather than make us hide the problem. I would bring two examples from my notebook to the steward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a scheduling app if required?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the app was the only way to see shifts, I would ask the steward or Jo to show me once. I have never used AI and do not want a bad tap on a phone to cost me Monday’s pay.

say: I would ask that **faster purchasing** reduce waste rather than raise every work target.
I would request **target figures** before the contractor changes how our work is judged.
think: My **slower pace** makes a counted-door target risky for my hours.
I worry **office staff** may lose work before any robot enters the site.
do: Put **target figures** on the union meeting agenda through the steward.
Keep taking **site shifts** during the first year.
Apply for **hospital maintenance** if clinic hours are cut.
feel: **Irritated** by screen counting and concerned for coworkers.
S1.quote: A warped frame can take half a day, and the count should show why rather than make us hide the problem.
fieldNote: Nikhil connects **office automation** to pressure on physical crews through narrow output counts.
He seeks **collective bargaining** and a conditional job application while continuing paid work.

steps.text: Ask the union steward to put new targets on the meeting agenda
Keep taking paid clinic site shifts in the first year
Apply for hospital maintenance if clinic hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the 2028 thinking system changes drawings before any machine can fit a real door, but that is only three years of space. I would want the union to demand paid notice and a retraining fund before robot trials start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when the office work changes, and cheaper plans could mean fewer mistakes but also fewer paid days on a tight contract. At 63 in 2031, capable robots could do the frames themselves; our savings could cover months, not a new working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the clinic shifts now and ask the steward for a meeting on written notice periods and paid training. In 2029 I would apply to two local building maintenance teams while still working the site; after 2031 I would ask the public employment office what income support we qualify for if robots replace us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be frightened, though I would not be without a first move. I hate needing public help, but wages cannot be wished back once the task is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apply to maintenance if robots can do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those jobs may last only until the robots become capable, and I would tell the teams that I can start now. An application in 2029 is about paid years before 2031, not a promise of safety afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jo tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Jo that I am still going to work tomorrow and that the three-month buffer is not a retirement fund. We would go through the bills together before deciding what help to seek.

say: I would say **thinking AI** changes drawings before robots fit doors.
I would ask the union for **paid notice** and a training fund before trials.
think: At **60**, cheap planning may reduce paid site days before physical robots arrive.
At **63**, robots could take door work and exhaust our buffer quickly.
do: Keep taking **clinic shifts** and seek a union meeting on notice.
Apply to **two maintenance teams** in 2029 while still employed.
Ask the **employment office** about income support if robots replace us.
feel: **Frightened**, but able to make a first move.
S2.quote: An application in 2029 is about paid years before 2031, not a promise of safety afterward.
fieldNote: Nikhil’s **three-month reserve** does not support years without work after robots reach carpentry tasks.
He treats maintenance as **temporary paid work** and public income support as a contingency after actual displacement.

steps.text: Keep taking paid clinic shifts through 2029
Ask the union steward for a meeting on notice and paid training
Apply to two local maintenance teams in 2029
Ask the public employment office about income support if robots replace the crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that five years is enough to negotiate proper notice while people are still needed on the site. I would ask the contractor to pay for any course it says workers must take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I may still fit frames while machines do the plans and inspections. At 66 in 2034, robots could take the fitting too, and I do not know whether any retirement payment would cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my site shifts and ask the union to get a written timetable for equipment changes. In 2032 I would apply for paid repairs at the municipal housing office if there is a vacancy, and I would enroll in the community college’s basic joinery class only if the contractor covers the fee and shift time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel more able to breathe than in the fast case, but I would still count the years. A course is useful to me only if it teaches a real skill and lets me keep earning while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the class need to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want someone to show me how to correct a twisted opening, not a stack of videos about perfect walls. I need supervised practice because I am still below the speed of the senior carpenters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for another construction job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are some sites nearby, and Jo’s care-home job is here, so I would search locally first. I would consider a move only after seeing a paid offer and what a new rent would cost.

say: I would ask for **written notice** while the site still needs workers.
I would expect the contractor to pay for **required courses**.
think: At **63**, physical fitting might continue after planning is automated.
At **66**, robots could take fitting before I know whether retirement income covers rent.
do: Keep **site shifts** and seek a union timetable for equipment changes.
Apply for **municipal housing repairs** in 2032 if a vacancy exists.
Enroll in **joinery class** only if fees and shift time are covered.
feel: **Breathing room**, paired with worry about the years left to earn.
S3.quote: A course is useful to me only if it teaches a real skill and lets me keep earning while I learn.
fieldNote: Nikhil will consider **supervised training** only when pay and fees protect current household income.
He keeps **local work** central because there are some nearby sites and Jo’s care-home wage anchors the household.

steps.text: Keep taking paid site shifts during 2032
Ask the union for a written equipment-change timetable
Apply for municipal housing repairs if a vacancy exists in 2032
Enroll in basic joinery only if the contractor covers fees and shift time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years gives the industry time to protect workers instead of springing a last-minute cut. I would press for a public list of employers that keep older apprentices working through the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I might have fewer heavy shifts because my back is not what it was. At 71 in 2039, capable robots could take the remaining site work, and a modest buffer cannot stand in for a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working the sites I can manage and add a small amount to savings in full-pay months. In 2037 I would review our household bills with Jo, ask the union to publish its list of employers retaining older apprentices, check my retirement statement, and apply for a lighter paid storekeeper opening if one is posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel less rushed but not settled. Ten years may let me reach retirement age, but it does not tell me what the rent will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would storekeeping survive the two waves of machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know whether AI would run the stock records or robots would shift the boxes. I would apply only for paid years if the job actually appeared, and I would not tell Jo it was secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the retirement statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the figure with our actual rent, food and care costs before cutting site days. If it falls short, I would keep looking for paid work that my back can handle.

say: I would ask for **older apprentices** to keep access to paid work.
I would press for a **public employer list** showing who actually retains them.
think: At **68**, my back may limit site shifts before thinking AI arrives.
At **71**, robots could end remaining work without solving our rent.
do: Keep **manageable site shifts** and add savings in full-pay months.
Review **bills and retirement figures** with Jo in 2037.
Apply for **lighter storekeeper work** if a paid opening appears.
feel: **Less rushed**, but still uncertain about future rent.
S4.quote: Ten years may let me reach retirement age, but it does not tell me what the rent will be.
fieldNote: Nikhil pairs the long warning with **physical aging** and refuses to treat retirement age as a guaranteed income.
His storekeeper application is **conditional** and explicitly exposed to both AI records and later physical robots.

steps.text: Keep taking site shifts his back can manage in 2037
Add a small amount to savings in full-pay months
Ask the union to publish its list of employers retaining older apprentices
Apply for a lighter paid storekeeper opening if posted
